newsitem.title: USA: Natural gas expands its U.S. base as vehicle fuel.
newsitem.headline: Natural gas expands its U.S. base as vehicle fuel.

text.p: Natural gas, no longer a novelty transportation fuel, is steadily building a base in the U.S. vehicle market, with cities increasingly turning to it as an ally in their fight against air pollution.
The number of gas-powered cars on U.S. roads hit 47,000 by the end of last year, according to the Chicago-based Gas Research Institute (GRI).
They estimate that number will swell to nearly 80,000 by the end of this year, a 41 percent increase.

Southern California, facing some of the country's worst smog problems, not surprisingly is leading the pack. Already there are more than 6,500 natural gas vehicles on the freeways of Los Angeles and San Diego.

"We are big supporters of natural gas usage in fleets. They are a great contribution in cleaning the air in crowded urban areas," said a spokeswoman from the Washington-based Natural Gas Supply Association (NGSA).
Nationally, natural gas-fueled vehicles have the potential of cutting carbon monoxide emissions by up to 90 percent and reactive hydrocarbon by up to 85 percent, the NGSA said.

Helping spur growth of natural gas as a transportation fuel are major engine manufacturers like Indiana-based Cummins Engine Co and Detroit Diesels, who have developed new engines for fleets of commuter buses, taxis and police cars.
Some, like Ford Motor Co, have developed dual-fueled vehicles, which let the driver switch to a backup gasoline tank when running low on natural gas.
Ford is putting four models on the market in 1997, one of which is dual-fueled.

Targetting fleets, like mail trucks, utility vans and city buses, makes the most sense, sources said, because the greatest economic and environmental benefits are to be had where the most fuel is burned.

Deploying fleets in urban areas also helps solve refueling problems. Natgas vehicles currently have about 1,100 refueling stations across the U.S., a number GRI estimates will nearly double to 2,000 by the year 2000.
New York City already has 20 stations, 12 of which are operated by the utility Brooklyn Union, a forerunner in the usage of natural gas in vehicles.
The company, citing strict new environmental legislation, predicted its efforts will cut air pollution in New York City alone by about 43 tons a year.

The law mandates that 80 percent of the city's light-duty vehicles purchased this year run on alternative fuels. Twenty percent of the city's new buses are also required to use an alternative to gasoline or diesel.

The company, which bought its first two natural gas vehicles back in 1988, currently has 800 gas vehicles on the road, 55 of which are commuter buses, out of the total of about 2,300 in New York City.

One advantage of natural gas over liquid fuel is the price, a Brooklyn Union spokesman said, adding 87-octane gasoline currently carries about a 20 percent premium to natural gas which, with a 120 octane rating, is a hotter-burning, more efficient fuel.
"You also don't have to worry about leaking tanks (at the stations) or freeze-ups in the winter," he said.
"Fuel lines freeze up on the gasoline vehicles, but we have never had that problem with the natural-gas vehicles," Brooklyn Union said in a news release.

The Environmental Protection Agency is currently reviewing standards that would require all U.S. automobiles produced after May 1998 to meet the low emission vehicle (LEV) standards that were instituted by California.
--H McCulloch, New York Power Desk +212-859-1628
